title: Leave your home empty for a month and your cover may already have changed
excerpt: Most home policies quietly restrict what they cover once a property has stood empty for a set number of days — often far sooner than people assume.
body: Most people picture home insurance as something that just keeps running in the background, covering the house whether they're in it or not. For a stretch of empty days, that's usually true. But every policy has an unoccupied-property clause, and once a home crosses that insurer's threshold for being empty, standard cover can be restricted or excluded — not paused, changed.

"Unoccupied" has a specific meaning here: no one staying overnight, not simply nobody home during the day. The exact number of days before the clause kicks in varies by insurer and by policy — it can be shorter than people expect, and it's stated in the policy wording, not advertised on the price comparison page.

What changes once a property is classed as unoccupied differs by insurer too, but it commonly narrows cover for things like escape of water, vandalism or malicious damage — exactly the kind of claim that's more likely to go unnoticed for longer in an empty home. It's rarely a case of the whole policy voiding outright, but the gap in what's actually covered can be significant.

If a property is going to sit empty for an extended period — a long trip, a probate property, a renovation between tenants — the fix is straightforward: tell the insurer before it happens. Many will extend cover for a fee or arrange specific unoccupied-property cover, and most also expect basics like regular check-ins and the water supply being turned off, so read exactly what's required alongside the day count.

It's worth checking this clause the same way you'd check the sum insured or single-item limits — not because it's likely to matter most years, but because it's exactly the kind of gap that only gets discovered at claim time.
